client: I’ve been feeling really anxious ever since I got assigned this major group project at university. I’m especially worried about the presentation part because I hate public speaking—it makes me feel like I’m going to freeze up or say something stupid. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this because it feels like such a specific problem, and I don’t know if talking about it will make my anxiety go away.
therapist: It sounds like this project is bringing up some intense worries, especially around public speaking—it’s completely valid to feel this way, and many people share similar concerns. Therapy can help by exploring the thoughts fueling your anxiety and finding strategies to manage them. What’s the worst-case scenario that comes to mind when you think about presenting?

client: The worst-case scenario? I guess I’m terrified I’ll completely blank out and embarrass myself in front of everyone. I keep imagining everyone staring at me, judging me, and thinking I’m incompetent. It’s hard to shake that image because it feels so real, like it’s definitely going to happen. I’m not sure how to stop thinking that way—it’s like my mind just spirals.
therapist: It’s understandable that your mind goes to this scenario—it sounds like it feels very vivid and overwhelming right now. Let’s take a step back and explore whether this worst-case scenario is a fact or a fear—what evidence do you have that this would actually happen? When you’ve been in similar situations before, how have they turned out?

client: I mean, I have given presentations before and I didn't completely freeze up, but I still messed up a few times—my voice shook and I forgot parts of my speech. People were nice about it, but I could tell they noticed. That's why I'm worried now, because even if the worst doesn't happen, just being visibly nervous feels humiliating. It's like I can't win.
therapist: It sounds like even though you’ve gotten through presentations before, the memory of feeling nervous sticks with you and makes this one feel daunting. What’s coming up for me is that being nervous doesn’t mean you’ve failed—it’s a natural response, and it sounds like others were understanding. How might it feel to shift the focus from avoiding nervousness to accepting that it’s part of the process?

client: I guess I never really thought about it that way. But even if nervousness is normal, it still feels like a weakness to me—like I should be able to control it better. Accepting it sounds nice in theory, but I worry that if I let myself be nervous, I'll just spiral even more during the actual presentation. Doesn't that make the anxiety worse?
therapist: It’s understandable to see nervousness as a weakness, especially when it feels so uncomfortable—but what if it’s not about controlling it completely, but about learning to work with it? Anxiety often feels worse when we fight it, but accepting it can actually help you feel more grounded. What might it look like to take small steps toward feeling okay with some nervousness, rather than trying to eliminate it entirely?

client: I see what you're saying, but it still feels really hard to accept nervousness as part of the process. What if I accept it and then it still overwhelms me during the presentation? I don’t want to feel like I’m giving up or not trying hard enough to improve. It’s like there’s this pressure to be perfect, even though I know that’s not realistic.
therapist: It sounds like accepting nervousness feels risky because you’re worried it might lead to feeling overwhelmed or like you’re not doing enough—that pressure to be perfect can be really heavy. What if we reframe acceptance as a strength, something that allows you to focus more on your message and less on trying to control every detail? How might it feel to let go of that perfectionism, even just a little?

client: I guess focusing on my message instead of perfection does sound like it would help, but it's hard to trust that. What if I mess up and people think I don't know my stuff? I've always believed that being flawless is the only way to be taken seriously. Letting that go even a little feels scary, like I'm lowering my standards.
therapist: It sounds like being flawless has felt like a safety net for you—like it’s the only way to ensure others take you seriously. That belief can be so heavy to carry, and it’s okay to feel scared about letting it go. What if we explored how much of this pressure to be flawless comes from you versus what others might actually expect? How might it feel to challenge that belief a little?

client: I never really thought about whether the pressure comes from me or others. I guess most people don't actually expect perfection - I've seen other students stumble in presentations and no one cared that much. But I still feel like I have to be better than that. Maybe it's more about my own standards? That makes it harder to change, because it's not like people are demanding perfection from me.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to recognize that the pressure to be perfect might be more about your own expectations than what others are actually asking of you—that’s a really important insight. It’s understandable that it feels harder to change when the standards are coming from within, but it also means you have the power to adjust them. What might it look like to set a more compassionate, realistic standard for yourself?

client: Setting a more compassionate standard sounds nice, but it feels really hard to do. I’ve always pushed myself to be the best, and letting that go feels like I’m settling or not living up to my potential. I guess I could try to aim for "good enough" instead of perfect, but I’m not sure how to do that without feeling like I’m failing.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a part of you that worries easing up on yourself might mean you’re settling or not reaching your potential—that’s a really common concern, especially when you’re used to pushing yourself so hard. What if shifting to “good enough” isn’t about settling, but about freeing up energy to focus on what truly matters? How might it feel to experiment with that mindset, even just in small ways?

client: I like the idea of freeing up energy, but it still feels like I'd be lying to myself if I said "good enough" was okay. What if I try it and then end up doing worse because I'm not pushing myself as hard? I don't know how to find a balance between being kind to myself and still maintaining high standards. It all just feels confusing and risky.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a fear that being kinder to yourself might lead to lower performance—that’s a valid concern, especially when you’re used to pushing yourself so much. What if we reframe self-compassion as a way to sustain your standards over time, rather than lowering them? How might it feel to explore small, manageable steps to balance kindness with ambition?

client: I guess reframing self-compassion as sustaining my standards makes sense, but it still feels abstract to me. I’m not sure what small, manageable steps would even look like—how do I start being kinder to myself without feeling like I’m letting myself off the hook? It’s hard to imagine how that would work in practice.
therapist: It’s completely understandable that this feels abstract right now—shifting how you relate to yourself takes time and practice. A small step could be noticing when you’re being harsh with yourself and asking, “Would I say this to a friend?” How might it feel to experiment with that question the next time you catch yourself pushing too hard?
